bible_refs.note: I will put a bridle in your nose, and a bit in your lips

choices.why: The verb καταλαζονεύω is rare and appears to mean 'to boast' or 'to vaunt' in this context, fitting the proud tone of the Assyrian's self-exaltation; alternatives like 'glories' or 'vaunts' were rejected as less idiomatic in English theological prose.

In this context, ἀνάπαυσις is explicitly equated with death later in the passage ('Rest, as I call it, he names death'), so 'rest' is used initially to preserve the author's ironic identification, avoiding premature interpretation; 'death' was rejected here to maintain the contrast before the explanation.

The paired terms ἔξοδος and εἴσοδος are a fixed biblical idiom (cf. Psalm 121:8) meaning the totality of one's movements or life; translating literally as 'exit and entrance' was rejected as too wooden, while 'departure and return' lost the communal, ongoing sense implied in the author's use.

φιμός here is clearly metaphorical for a bridle (as paired with χαλινός, 'bit'), referring to divine control over the proud Assyrian; 'muzzle' was rejected because it does not pair naturally with 'bit' in the context of governing animals or nations, and the following clause confirms the equestrian metaphor.

How? But you, holding vainly upon nothing, did you not hear these things long ago, which I did? For if indeed you wish, he says, to busy yourselves with the words of my prophets, I already said, anticipating, that these things will come to be. For I from ancient days set in order, that is, I ordained and I inclined; but I have shown now the season calling to the end the things foretold, so as to lay waste nations in fortified cities, that is, not weak, and vulnerable; I stretched out my hands, and they were dried up. For the one who formerly held them together against being, and caused the avenging hand to stand, I removed, and in equal grass they were dried up, and like grass they withered, and like what someone as dry straw gives nourishment to fire. This also he says elsewhere to him. For since the things ordained to happen by God the impious passing through has considered himself greatly, again he heard God saying: 'Will the axe be glorified apart from the one hewing in it? Or will the saw be exalted apart from the one drawing it?' For just as these instruments do not move themselves to works by chance, but wait rather for the hand of the one shaking; so you, he says, have become an instrument of the divine wrath, but you yourself did not work by your powers, but you were rather like an axe, and a saw, appointed to serve the will of the one moving. Now then, I know your rest, and your going out.

But your wrath, which you were angry, and your bitterness came up against me. He says, therefore, being made a servant of the divine judgments, he boasts, perhaps thinking against himself, and alone he thinks to be magnified by these nations and regions, as he has burned them and taken them. But I know your rest, and your going out, and your coming in. Rest, as I call it, he names death, and going out and coming in, the way into every thing of the deeds. For nothing at all escapes the mind that knows all things. Adding, that your wrath, which you were angry, and your bitterness came up against me, he alone says, You will not be unpunished for having been slandered. For I will not at all look upon your wicked thoughts, the evil and bitter, but as one provoked to grief by your dispositions, I will impose upon them their proper justice. And I will put a bridle in your nose, and a bit in your lips, and I will turn you back by the way by which you came. Since the Assyrian, having the folly of beasts most conspicuously, mocked God, and as it were having rushed into wildness like a beast, he sent forth the sounds of the glory of God, in this way moreover very fittingly as concerning beasts he says, I will put a bridle in your nose, and a bit in your lips, not only by the leadings of the plagues.
pass_b_english: How is it that you, grasping at nothing but vanity, did you not hear these things long ago—the very things I have done? If you truly desire to occupy yourselves with the words of my prophets, I have already declared, even before they came to pass, that these events would occur. For from the earliest days I have established and ordained all things, setting them in their proper order.

Now I have revealed the appointed time, when the foretold judgments come to their fulfillment, so that nations shall be laid waste even in their fortified cities—not the weak, but the strong and seemingly secure. I stretched out my hands, and they withered and dried up.

He who once held them together, sustaining them in existence and establishing the hand that avenges, I have removed; and now the grass withers equally, the herbs fade like straw, and the dry stalks become fuel for the fire.

Thus also he says elsewhere to him: Since the impious, passing through what God has ordained, has grown proud in his own heart, he again heard God saying, 'Shall the axe boast itself against the one who hews with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself above the one who draws it?' For just as these tools do not move themselves to work by chance, but wait for the hand that shakes them, so you have become an instrument of my divine wrath.
Yet you did not act by your own strength; you were like an axe and a saw, moved only by the will of the one who uses you. And now I know your rest and your going out.

Your wrath, which you once burned with, and your bitterness have risen up against me. He boasts, having become a servant of the divine judgments, perhaps imagining in his heart that he alone has been magnified by conquering these nations and lands, as he has burned them and taken them captive. But I know your rest, and your going out, and your coming in.

He calls rest what I name death, and going out and coming in, the way to every undertaking. For nothing at all escapes the mind that knows all things. He adds, saying that your wrath, which you once burned with, and your bitterness have risen up against me, that you shall not go unpunished for having been slandered.

For I will not at all look upon your wicked thoughts, the evil and the bitter, but as one provoked to grief by your dispositions, I will impose upon them their proper justice. And I will put a bridle in your nose, and a bit in your lips, and I will turn you back by the way by which you came.

Since the Assyrian, having the folly of beasts most conspicuously, mocked God, and as it were having rushed into wildness like a beast, he sent forth the sounds of the glory of God, in this way moreover very fittingly as concerning beasts he says, I will put a bridle in your nose, and a bit in your lips, not only by the leadings of the plagues.
